name: Aoki Lock Control
description: Aoki Lock Control captures a turned-out foot against the attacker's upper body while the legs manage the opponent's hip, preparing a rotational foot lock that can also stress the knee.
summary: Aoki Lock Control captures a turned-out foot against the attacker's upper body while the legs manage the opponent's hip, preparing a rotational foot lock that can also stress the knee.
overview:
The foot-lock player is seated or on the side facing the opponent's lower body. The opposing foot is turned outward and enclosed near the armpit, upper arm, and forearm. The attacker has a connection to the hip or leg that limits the opponent's free movement. The captured player must free the foot and leg control before attempting an uncontrolled turn.

The captured limb is the foot and lower leg. This is distinct from an omoplata-style shoulder trap and from a bent-knee calf slicer. Either player can become the foot-lock attacker during an entanglement exchange. Terminology: Aoki foot-lock control.

Recognize the foot orientation without twisting it into position against resistance. Hold the instep and heel region securely beside the upper body rather than relying on calf compression. Use the entanglement or foot-on-hip frame to manage distance before considering a finish.

Rotational foot locks can injure the ankle or knee before pain provides useful warning. Use cooperative capture-and-release practice, no spinning escapes, and the event's actual division rules.

Instructional sources: [Stephan Kesting and Rob Biernacki — the Aoki lock](https://www.grapplearts.com/the-step-by-step-aoki-lock/); [IBJJF — current rule resources](https://ibjjf.com/books-videos).
key_principles: Identify the turned foot: Recognize the foot orientation without twisting it into position against resistance.
Enclose the foot: Hold the instep and heel region securely beside the upper body rather than relying on calf compression.
Control the hip connection: Use the entanglement or foot-on-hip frame to manage distance before considering a finish.
Keep pressure neutral: Stop the drill at a secure capture; the control can become a damaging rotation with very little movement.
Respect counterattacks: Keep track of your own exposed feet while concentrating on the captured foot.
Release before rotation: Open the arm enclosure and remove leg pressure immediately on a tap, sudden movement, or pain.

top.overview:
The top player is responsible for recognizing and defending the control. The foot-lock player is seated or on the side facing the opponent's lower body. The opposing foot is turned outward and enclosed near the armpit, upper arm, and forearm. The attacker has a connection to the hip or leg that limits the opponent's free movement. The captured player must free the foot and leg control before attempting an uncontrolled turn.

A turned-out foot enclosed beside the armpit is a rotational threat, not simply a straight ankle-lock grip. Prevent the foot enclosure and recover leg position while the opponent still lacks a secure connection. Do not spin the torso while the foot remains fixed.

Address the upper-body grip before withdrawing the leg through a tight entanglement. Tap early to a secure rotational lock rather than treating the absence of pain as safety. Separate the feet and restore a stable guard or standing base before resuming movement.

The captured limb is the foot and lower leg. This is distinct from an omoplata-style shoulder trap and from a bent-knee calf slicer. Either player can become the foot-lock attacker during an entanglement exchange. Rotational foot locks can injure the ankle or knee before pain provides useful warning. Use cooperative capture-and-release practice, no spinning escapes, and the event's actual division rules.

flashcards.question: Aoki defense: which foot position warns that this is more than a straight ankle lock?
flashcards.answer: A turned-out foot enclosed beside the armpit is a rotational threat, not simply a straight ankle-lock grip.

plausible: Toes straight along their forearm
Sole flat on the mat below the hips
trap: Heel free; only the calf squeezed

flashcards.question: Aoki defense: what should your hands address before the opponent closes the grip?
flashcards.answer: Prevent the foot enclosure and recover leg position while the opponent still lacks a secure connection.
flashcards.answer_line: The arm wrapping around your foot

plausible: Their foot on your hip alone
Post behind you and pull the leg
trap: Counterattack their far leg first

flashcards.question: Aoki defense: why is turning your torso dangerous while the foot remains captured?
flashcards.answer: Do not spin the torso while the foot remains fixed.
flashcards.answer_line: The fixed foot loads knee rotation

plausible: The ankle absorbs all turning force
The heel slips free before the turn
trap: The foot follows your shoulders

flashcards.question: Aoki defense: which connection must open before you pull the trapped leg away?
flashcards.answer: Address the upper-body grip before withdrawing the leg through a tight entanglement.
flashcards.answer_line: Their arm enclosure on your foot

plausible: Their hip-posting leg alone
The gap between your own knees
trap: Their far-leg hook alone

flashcards.question: Aoki defense: the grip is secure but painless; what makes continuing risky?
flashcards.answer: Tap early to a secure rotational lock rather than treating the absence of pain as safety.

plausible: Only calf compression causes damage
A bent knee absorbs the turn safely
trap: No pain means the foot can rotate

flashcards.question: Aoki defense: after the opponent opens the lock, what precedes resuming the exchange?
flashcards.answer: Separate the feet and restore a stable guard or standing base before resuming movement.
flashcards.answer_line: Free both feet; rebuild your base

plausible: Leave the heel in their armpit
Turn away with the hip still held
trap: Pull back with the toes enclosed

flashcards.question: Aoki defense: in the reviewed seated setup, where is the foot-locker relative to your legs?
flashcards.answer: The foot-lock player is seated or on the side facing the opponent's lower body.
flashcards.answer_line: Facing your legs, seated or side-on

plausible: Beside your knee, out of foot reach

trap: Over your thighs, foot far from ribs

flashcards.question: Aoki control: what orientation of the captured foot gives the lock its rotational character?
flashcards.answer: Recognize the foot orientation without twisting it into position against resistance.
flashcards.answer_line: Foot turned outward inside the arms

plausible: Toes aligned with the kneecap
Sole pointing straight at the mat
trap: Ankle free while the calf folds

flashcards.question: Aoki control: where should you secure the opponent's instep and heel?
flashcards.answer: Hold the instep and heel region securely beside the upper body rather than relying on calf compression.
flashcards.answer_line: Close beside your ribs and armpit

plausible: Between your knees, arms extended
Across your shoulder, heel loose
trap: At your chest but free to slide

flashcards.question: Aoki control: what prevents the opponent moving the hip freely away from your grip?
flashcards.answer: Use the entanglement or foot-on-hip frame to manage distance before considering a finish.

plausible: Heel grip without thigh contact
Ankle pull with both arms extended
trap: Calf squeeze without a hip anchor

flashcards.question: Aoki control: when should a cooperative capture drill stop adding load?
flashcards.answer: Stop the drill at a secure capture; the control can become a damaging rotation with very little movement.
flashcards.answer_line: When the turned foot is enclosed

plausible: When the knee visibly rotates
When their hip lifts off the mat
trap: When calf pressure becomes painful

flashcards.question: Aoki control: which of your foot placements can feed the reciprocal counter?
flashcards.answer: While controlling one leg, do not overlook your own hip-posting foot. Kesting shows that exposed post being collected for an Aoki counter.
flashcards.answer_line: The reachable foot on their hip

plausible: A foot hidden behind your knee
A foot withdrawn behind your hip
trap: A distant mat post, toes turned away

flashcards.question: Aoki control: what should open immediately when the partner signals a stop?
flashcards.answer: Open the arm enclosure and remove leg pressure immediately on a tap, sudden movement, or pain.
flashcards.answer_line: The arm clamp and leg pressure

plausible: Only the hand nearest their toes
Only the foot away from their hip
trap: The elbows, with knees still turning

flashcards.question: Aoki control: in the reviewed seated capture, what should your torso face?
flashcards.answer: The foot-lock player is seated or on the side facing the opponent's lower body.
flashcards.answer_line: Toward the opponent's hips and legs

plausible: Away, with the foot behind your hips
Toward their chest, foot far away
trap: Down, with heel outside your arms

flashcards.answer_line: The enclosed, turned foot is a lever

plausible: A bent knee folds over a shin
Heel pulled to the same-side hip
trap: Calf compressed with the ankle free
